domains.name: Core 1: Hardware, Networking & Mobile Devices
domains.summary: Motherboards, CPUs, RAM, storage, power, peripherals, printers, TCP/IP, Wi-Fi, SOHO networking, and mobile devices — the physical and network foundation (220-1201).

scenarios.title: The RAM Upgrade That Won't POST
scenarios.situation: A friend's desktop has 8 GB of DDR3 and feels slow. They bought a cheap 16 GB DDR4 kit online and installed it. Now the PC powers on — fans spin, no display — and the motherboard emits a repeating long-beep POST code. The DDR4 stick visibly does not sit flush in the slot.
scenarios.prompt: What is the cause, and what is the correct fix?
evidence: POST beep codes
A repeating long-beep pattern with no display typically signals a memory fault detected during the Power-On Self-Test, before any video initializes.
DDR3 vs DDR4

DDR3 DIMMs are 240-pin at 1.5V; DDR4 DIMMs are 288-pin at 1.2V. The keying notch sits in a different position, so a DDR4 stick cannot seat in a DDR3 slot. The two generations are electrically and physically incompatible — no BIOS update changes the slot.
choices: The DDR4 kit is incompatible with a DDR3 board — remove it and install DDR3 (240-pin) memory matched to the board instead.
Force the DDR4 stick fully into the slot until the clips engage; the notch difference is cosmetic.
Flash the motherboard BIOS — a newer BIOS adds DDR4 support to DDR3 boards.
Install the DDR4 in the second channel slots; the first channel only accepts DDR3.
scenarios.why: DDR3 and DDR4 differ in pin count, voltage, and notch position, so the stick physically cannot seat — the beep code is the board telling you memory failed POST. Forcing it risks cracking the slot or shorting pins. The fix is memory of the generation the board was built for (DDR3), ideally as a matched pair for dual-channel operation.
scenarios.hint: Can a firmware update change the shape of a physical slot?

scenarios.title: The Shutdown After Ten Minutes
scenarios.situation: A gaming PC shuts off abruptly about ten minutes into any game, then powers back on fine. The BIOS hardware monitor shows the CPU at 96°C just before shutdown; the CPU fan is barely turning and rattles. The case interior is otherwise clean.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause and the correct first fix?
evidence: Thermal protection

Modern CPUs throttle performance as temperatures climb, then trigger an emergency shutdown around 95–100°C to prevent silicon damage. A shutdown that always follows sustained load is the classic thermal signature.
The cooling stack
The heatsink/fan assembly must make firm, even contact with the CPU through thermal paste. A failing fan — or dried-out paste — breaks heat transfer, and temperatures spike within minutes under load.
choices: Replace the failing CPU fan (reapplying thermal paste while the heatsink is off), then confirm temperatures stay in range under load.
Increase the PSU wattage; shutdowns under load are always a power problem.
Disable thermal throttling in BIOS so the CPU can run hotter without shutting down.
Reinstall Windows; random shutdowns are caused by corrupt system files.
scenarios.why: 96°C before shutdown with a rattling, slow fan is a textbook cooling failure — the CPU is protecting itself. Replacing the fan restores airflow, and fresh thermal paste restores heat transfer since the heatsink must come off anyway. A PSU issue would not track CPU temperature; disabling throttling invites permanent damage; and an OS reinstall cannot fix a thermal fault.
scenarios.hint: What does the temperature reading tell you about power vs. heat?

scenarios.title: RAID for the Two-Disk NAS
scenarios.situation: A small office buys a 2-bay NAS with two 4 TB drives. They want the most usable capacity possible WITHOUT losing data if one drive fails. They ask whether to configure RAID 0, RAID 1, or RAID 5.
scenarios.prompt: Which RAID level fits, and why are the others wrong?
evidence: RAID levels

RAID 0 stripes data across disks: usable capacity is the sum of all disks, with NO redundancy — one disk failure destroys the array. RAID 1 mirrors: usable capacity equals one disk, survives a single-disk failure, needs exactly 2 disks. RAID 5 stripes with distributed parity: usable capacity is (n−1) disks and it requires a minimum of 3 disks.
choices: RAID 1 — it mirrors both disks and survives one failure; RAID 0 has no redundancy and RAID 5 needs at least 3 disks.
RAID 0 — striping doubles usable capacity and protects against a single-disk failure.
RAID 5 — parity works fine on two disks when enabled in software.
RAID 1 — and it doubles usable capacity compared to a single disk.
scenarios.why: With two disks, RAID 1 is the only level that both survives a disk failure and is valid: you get 4 TB usable, fully mirrored. RAID 0 gives 8 TB but zero fault tolerance — the opposite of the requirement. RAID 5 is not configurable on two disks (minimum three). And RAID 1 never doubles capacity; mirroring costs half the raw space.
scenarios.hint: Which levels are even valid with exactly two disks?

scenarios.title: New GPU, Random Reboots
scenarios.situation: After installing a graphics card rated at 200 W TDP into a PC with a 450 W budget PSU — already powering a 95 W CPU and three drives — the system hard-reboots during gaming but is perfectly stable at idle. Voltages look normal in BIOS at idle.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause and the correct fix?
evidence: PSU sizing

Add component TDPs and leave roughly 20–30% headroom. Here 95 W (CPU) + 200 W (GPU) + drives and board lands near 350 W before headroom — a 450 W budget unit is marginal, and cheap units often cannot sustain their label rating. An undersized PSU trips over-current protection under load, causing instant hard reboots.
PSU connectors
GPUs draw through dedicated 6-pin and 8-pin PCIe power connectors. A PSU without native PCIe connectors — or one relying on Molex/SATA adapters — is a red flag for GPU upgrades.
choices: The PSU is undersized and marginal — replace it with a quality 650 W or larger unit with native PCIe connectors.
Undervolt the CPU in BIOS; reboots under load are always CPU voltage issues.
Reinstall the GPU drivers; driver crashes cause hard reboots.
Add more case fans; the PSU is shutting down from heat, not load.
scenarios.why: Stable at idle plus instant reboots under load is the signature of a PSU hitting its limit when the GPU ramps up — idle voltage readings cannot catch it. Sizing math confirms the 450 W unit has no headroom. A quality 650 W unit with native PCIe connectors solves both capacity and connector concerns; drivers and fans do not explain load-dependent hard reboots.
scenarios.hint: When exactly does it reboot — at idle, or when the GPU wakes up?

scenarios.title: Locking Down the SOHO Router
scenarios.situation: You are setting up a home-office router. Out of the box it broadcasts the default SSID, the admin password is still 'admin', WPS is enabled, the wireless security is set to legacy WPA (TKIP), and remote management is open to the internet.
evidence: SOHO router hardening

Change the default admin credentials; use WPA3 — or WPA2 with AES if the hardware lacks WPA3; disable WPS (its PIN is brute-forceable); disable remote management from the WAN side; update the firmware; use a long, unique passphrase on the SSID.
What does not secure you
Hiding the SSID and MAC filtering are trivially bypassed by anyone with a packet sniffer. WEP is broken and must never be used.
choices: Change the default admin password, set WPA3 (or WPA2-AES) with a strong passphrase, disable WPS and WAN-side remote management, and update the firmware.
Hide the SSID and enable MAC filtering — that alone secures the network.
Switch to WEP with a long key; WEP's longer keys are effectively unbreakable.
Leave the defaults but install antivirus on every device; endpoint protection replaces router hardening.
scenarios.why: The highest-value fixes attack the real weaknesses: guessable admin credentials, weak encryption, brute-forceable WPS, and an internet-exposed management interface. SSID hiding and MAC filtering are security theater against real tools, WEP is cryptographically broken, and antivirus cannot compensate for a compromised gateway.
scenarios.hint: Which of these would stop someone who already knows how to sniff wireless traffic?

scenarios.title: The 169.254 Address
scenarios.situation: A Windows PC reports 'No internet'. Running `ipconfig` shows IPv4 address 169.254.23.7 with no default gateway. Other PCs on the same switch work fine, and the cable's link light is on.
scenarios.prompt: What does the 169.254.x.x address mean, and what is the next troubleshooting step?
evidence: APIPA

When Windows cannot reach a DHCP server, it self-assigns an address in 169.254.0.0/16 (APIPA — Automatic Private IP Addressing). An APIPA address means DHCP failed; it is not a usable LAN or internet address. A lit link light means Layer 1 (the cable) is up.
The DHCP recovery workflow
`ipconfig /release` followed by `ipconfig /renew` forces a fresh DHCP request. `ping 127.0.0.1` verifies the local TCP/IP stack independently of the network.
choices: APIPA means DHCP failed — run `ipconfig /release` then `ipconfig /renew`, then check the DHCP server/service and the switch port or VLAN for this PC.
169.254.x.x is a valid public IP — the ISP must be down, so wait it out.
Assign a static IP in the 169.254 range; APIPA addresses route to the internet normally.
Replace the NIC immediately; an APIPA address always means dead hardware.
scenarios.why: 169.254.23.7 is APIPA — the PC asked for DHCP and got no answer — while other PCs work, so the DHCP server is up and the fault is local to this machine or its port. Forcing a renew is the fast test; if it still fails, suspect the DHCP client service, a bad cable/port, or a VLAN mismatch. APIPA never routes to the internet and does not by itself condemn the NIC.
scenarios.hint: The other PCs work — what does that tell you about the DHCP server?

scenarios.title: Slow Wi-Fi in the Apartment
scenarios.situation: A laptop connected on the 2.4 GHz band gets 15 Mbps in a crowded apartment building, while the wired PC on the same internet plan gets 400 Mbps. The router also broadcasts 5 GHz and supports 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6).
evidence: Bands and standards

2.4 GHz travels farther and penetrates walls better, but it has only three non-overlapping channels (1, 6, and 11) — in a crowded building, neighbor networks interfere heavily. 5 GHz offers many more channels and higher throughput at shorter range. 802.11n = Wi-Fi 4, 802.11ac = Wi-Fi 5, 802.11ax = Wi-Fi 6 (and 6E in the 6 GHz band).
Security baseline
Whatever band you use, the network should run WPA3 or WPA2 with AES — never WEP.
choices: Move the laptop to the 5 GHz SSID (keeping WPA2/WPA3 security) — more clear channels and far higher throughput near the router.
Switch the router to WEP to reduce encryption overhead and gain speed.
Buy a bigger antenna; 2.4 GHz is always faster than 5 GHz.
Disable the 5 GHz radio to force every device onto the longer-range band.
scenarios.why: The laptop's bottleneck is 2.4 GHz congestion, not the internet plan — the wired PC proves 400 Mbps is available. 5 GHz sidesteps the crowded 2.4 GHz channels and delivers the throughput the plan offers. WEP would destroy security for no real gain, and disabling 5 GHz removes the exact band that fixes the problem.
scenarios.hint: The wired PC gets full speed — where is the bottleneck?

scenarios.title: Ghosting on the Laser Printer
scenarios.situation: A shared laser printer prints faint repeating ghost images of previous pages down each sheet, and paper occasionally jams near the fuser. The toner cartridge was replaced last month and prints are otherwise dark.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely failed component, and what is the safe fix?
evidence: The laser printing process

The drum holds the latent image that toner adheres to; the fuser then melts toner onto the paper with high heat. A worn drum fails to fully discharge between rotations, leaving ghost images that repeat at drum-circumference intervals. Drums, fusers, and rollers are wear items sold as a scheduled maintenance kit.
Fuser safety
The fuser runs near 200°C — hot enough to burn skin instantly. Always power the printer off and let the fuser cool before touching it, and follow the manufacturer's maintenance-kit procedure.
choices: Worn drum / maintenance kit — power off, let the fuser cool completely, then install the manufacturer's maintenance kit (drum, fuser, rollers).
Replace the toner again; ghosting is always caused by low toner.
Open the printer mid-print to watch exactly where the jam happens.
Blow compressed air into the hot fuser to clear the jam quickly.
scenarios.why: Repeating ghost images at fixed intervals with fresh toner points at the drum, not the cartridge — and jams at the fuser point at worn rollers/fuser, which is exactly what the scheduled maintenance kit replaces. Opening a running printer or touching a hot fuser risks injury and damage; the safe, correct fix is a powered-off, cooled-down maintenance-kit replacement.
scenarios.hint: The toner is new and prints are dark — what else in the imaging chain wears out?

domains.name: Core 2: Operating Systems, Security & Procedures
domains.summary: Windows installation and administration, macOS and Linux basics, malware removal, access control, encryption, social engineering, and the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology (220-1202).

scenarios.title: Windows 11 Install Checklist
scenarios.situation: You are clean-installing Windows 11 on a brand-new NVMe SSD. The motherboard is currently in Legacy/CSM boot mode, and the disk was initialized as MBR. Setup flags requirement problems before it will proceed.
scenarios.prompt: What must change for a proper Windows 11 installation?
evidence: Windows 11 requirements
Windows 11 requires a 64-bit CPU, UEFI firmware (not Legacy/CSM), Secure Boot capability, TPM 2.0, a GPT-partitioned system disk, 4 GB of RAM, and 64 GB of storage.
Disk preparation
In the installer command prompt, `diskpart` followed by `select disk`, `clean`, and `convert gpt` prepares the disk; the installer then creates the EFI system partition on GPT automatically.
choices: Enable UEFI mode, TPM 2.0, and Secure Boot in firmware, and convert the disk to GPT (e.g., with diskpart) before installing.
Keep Legacy/CSM and MBR — Windows 11 installs fine on BIOS/MBR systems.
Disable TPM 2.0; it conflicts with NVMe drives.
Format the SSD as FAT32; NTFS is deprecated for Windows 11.
scenarios.why: Windows 11's installer enforces UEFI + Secure Boot + TPM 2.0 + GPT — Legacy/CSM with MBR fails those checks by design. Converting the disk to GPT and switching the firmware to UEFI mode satisfies every requirement at once. TPM does not conflict with NVMe, and Windows still installs to NTFS.
scenarios.hint: Which firmware mode does Windows 11 actually require?
objectives: GPT vs MBR, UEFI vs Legacy

scenarios.title: Pop-ups and a Hijacked Homepage
scenarios.situation: A user's PC shows constant pop-ups, the browser homepage changed itself overnight, and new toolbars appeared. Task Manager shows an unfamiliar process consuming CPU.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct FIRST response under the CompTIA malware-removal procedure?
evidence: Malware removal procedure (CompTIA best practice)

1. Investigate and verify symptoms. 2. Quarantine infected systems. 3. Disable System Restore (in Windows). 4. Remediate infected systems. 5. Schedule scans and updates. 6. Enable System Restore and create a restore point (in Windows). 7. Educate the end user.
choices: Investigate and verify the symptoms first, then quarantine the machine from the network before remediating.
Immediately delete the unfamiliar process's files and empty the Recycle Bin.
Disable System Restore first — that is always step one.
Reinstall Windows right away; investigation wastes time.
scenarios.why: The procedure opens with investigation and verification — you must confirm what you are dealing with before acting — followed by quarantine so the infection cannot spread or phone home while you work. Deleting files blind risks breaking the system, System Restore is disabled at step 3 (not step 1), and a reinstall skips quarantine and wastes the chance to learn the infection vector.
scenarios.hint: What does the procedure list before quarantine?

scenarios.title: The Six Steps, in Order
scenarios.situation: A junior tech fixed a printer by swapping parts until it worked, never tested anything else, and wrote nothing down. Their lead asks them to follow the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology next time.
scenarios.prompt: Which sequence IS the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology?
evidence: CompTIA 6-step troubleshooting methodology

1. Identify the problem. 2. Establish a theory of probable cause. 3. Test the theory to determine the cause. 4. Establish a plan of action to resolve the problem and implement the solution. 5. Verify full system functionality and, if applicable, implement preventive measures. 6. Document findings, actions, and outcomes.
choices: Identify the problem, establish a theory of probable cause, test the theory, establish a plan of action and implement the solution, verify full system functionality and add preventive measures, document findings and outcomes.
Replace parts until it works, verify briefly, document only if there is time.
Document first, then identify, test, implement, theorize, and verify.
Establish a theory, identify the problem, implement the fix, test, document, verify.
scenarios.why: The methodology is deliberately ordered: you cannot theorize before identifying, cannot plan before testing the theory, and must verify the whole system — not just the symptom — before documenting. The junior tech's swap-until-it-works approach skips theory, testing, full verification, and documentation, which is exactly what the lead wants fixed.
scenarios.hint: Theory comes before action — but what comes before theory?

scenarios.title: "Permission Denied" on the Deploy Script
scenarios.situation: On a Linux workstation, running `./deploy.sh` returns 'Permission denied' even though you own the file. `ls -l` shows the permissions as `-rw-r--r--`.
evidence: Linux file permissions

`ls -l` output `-rw-r--r--` means the owner has read and write but NOT execute permission. Adding the execute bit with `chmod +x deploy.sh` (or `chmod 755 deploy.sh` for rwxr-xr-x) makes the script runnable.
choices: Add the execute bit with `chmod +x deploy.sh` (or `chmod 755 deploy.sh`), then run it again.
Run `chmod 000 deploy.sh` to reset the permissions.
Delete and re-download the script; permissions cannot be changed on files you own.
Run `sudo rm deploy.sh` to bypass the permission check.
scenarios.why: `-rw-r--r--` is missing the `x` (execute) bit, which is exactly why the shell refuses to run it. `chmod +x` sets that bit for the owner. `chmod 000` would remove all access, re-downloading is pointless since you own the file and can change its mode, and `rm` deletes the script rather than fixing it.
scenarios.hint: Read the permission string character by character — which letter is missing?

scenarios.title: RDP Dies at the Firewall
scenarios.situation: Remote Desktop to a server worked until a firewall rule change. `ping` to the server still succeeds, but the RDP client times out. The firewall log shows drops on the RDP port.
scenarios.prompt: Which port must the firewall allow, and over which protocol?
evidence: Common ports
RDP = TCP 3389. SSH = TCP 22. HTTPS = TCP 443. DNS = UDP/TCP 53. SMB = TCP 445. Ping uses ICMP, not TCP — a successful ping proves nothing about whether TCP 3389 is open.
choices: TCP 3389 — the RDP port; ping only proves ICMP is open.
UDP 3389 — RDP is UDP-only.
TCP 443 — Remote Desktop tunnels over HTTPS by default.
TCP 22 — Remote Desktop uses the SSH port.
scenarios.why: RDP listens on TCP 3389, and the firewall log confirms drops on exactly that port — the rule change blocked it. Ping succeeding is a red herring: ICMP and TCP are filtered independently. 443 is HTTPS, 22 is SSH, and RDP is TCP-based (UDP 3389 is only an optional transport enhancement).
scenarios.hint: Ping uses ICMP — what protocol does the RDP client actually need?

scenarios.title: The "IT Support" Phone Call
scenarios.situation: A user receives a call from 'IT support' claiming their account is compromised and asking for their password and MFA code to 'verify' them. The caller ID looks like an internal number.
scenarios.prompt: What is this attack, and what should the user do?
evidence: Social engineering

Vishing (voice phishing) uses phone calls — often with spoofed caller ID — to steal credentials. Legitimate IT staff never ask for passwords or MFA codes; anyone who does is an attacker by definition. Verify through a known-good channel and report the attempt to security.
choices: It is vishing — hang up, share nothing, and report it to IT/security through a known-good contact method.
Comply with the request — the internal-looking caller ID proves they are legitimate IT.
Give them the password but withhold the MFA code; that is a safe compromise.
Ask them to call back tomorrow so there is time to think it over.
scenarios.why: Caller ID is trivially spoofed, so it proves nothing — and the request itself is the giveaway, because real IT never asks for passwords or MFA codes. Hanging up and reporting through a verified channel both stops this attempt and lets security warn others. Partial compliance still hands over the password.
scenarios.hint: Would real IT ever ask for your MFA code?

scenarios.title: Crashes, Disk Errors, and a Repair Plan
scenarios.situation: A Windows PC boots but applications crash randomly. Event Viewer (Windows Logs → System) shows repeated disk errors from the Disk source. You ran `sfc /scannow`, which reported corrupt files it could not repair.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct repair sequence?
evidence: Repair tools

`sfc /scannow` verifies and repairs protected Windows system files from the component store. `chkdsk C: /r` locates bad sectors and recovers readable data (it implies /f, fixing filesystem errors too). Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc) is where you confirm whether faults are hardware or software in origin.
Order of operations

Fix the underlying disk BEFORE repairing system files — running sfc against a failing disk just writes fresh files onto bad sectors. Back up data before `chkdsk /r` on a suspect drive, since a dying disk can fail completely under the scan's stress.
choices: Back up data first, run `chkdsk C: /r` to address the bad sectors, then re-run `sfc /scannow`; if errors persist, plan a drive replacement.
Run `sfc /scannow` repeatedly until it passes; the disk errors are unrelated to the corrupt files.
Run `diskpart clean` on the drive and reinstall — the fastest fix.
Disable the Disk source in Event Viewer so the errors stop appearing.
scenarios.why: Event Viewer proves the root cause is the disk, so sfc's failure is a symptom — corrupt files keep landing on bad sectors. The correct order is: protect the data (backup), repair the disk surface (`chkdsk /r`), then repair system files (`sfc /scannow`) onto a now-stable disk. `diskpart clean` would destroy the user's data, and silencing Event Viewer hides the fault instead of fixing it.
scenarios.hint: sfc failed — is the corruption the disease or a symptom?

scenarios.title: The Stolen Sales Laptop
scenarios.situation: A salesperson's laptop holding customer PII was stolen from a car. It had no full-disk encryption, no sign-in password, and a standard removable SATA SSD. Management asks which control would have protected the data.
scenarios.prompt: Which combination would have protected the data at rest?
evidence: Encryption at rest

Full-disk encryption (BitLocker on Windows, FileVault on macOS) renders the entire drive unreadable without the decryption key — even if the drive is pulled and mounted in another machine. TPM-backed BitLocker ties the key to the device hardware. A login password alone does not stop drive removal; EFS encrypts individual files, not the whole disk.
Defense in depth
No single control is enough: combine encryption with strong authentication, and add remote-wipe capability for mobile devices that leave the office.
choices: BitLocker full-disk encryption (TPM-backed) plus a strong sign-in — a removed drive is unreadable without the key.
A strong Windows login password alone — the drive cannot be read without logging in.
EFS on the Documents folder — equivalent protection to full-disk encryption.
Antivirus with real-time protection — it encrypts the drive automatically.
scenarios.why: A thief can simply pull an unencrypted SSD and read it in another machine — no login password stops that, and antivirus does not encrypt anything. BitLocker encrypts every sector, so the removed drive is ciphertext without the TPM-backed key. EFS only covers selected files and leaves the rest of the disk (temp files, pagefile, slack space) exposed.
scenarios.hint: What stops someone who never boots your OS at all?

lessons.title: Network triage: from cable to cloud in five commands
concepts: Every network problem lives on a layer. Start at the bottom: is the cable plugged in and the link light on? A lit link light with no connectivity means Layer 1 is fine and the fault is logical — usually addressing, DHCP, or DNS. This bottom-up habit keeps you from reinstalling drivers for a DHCP outage.

`ipconfig /all` is your map. It shows the IPv4 address, subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS servers. A 169.254.x.x address with no gateway is APIPA — Windows telling you DHCP failed. A correct-looking 192.168.x.x address with a gateway shifts suspicion to DNS or beyond the LAN.

The ping ladder isolates the fault by climbing outward: `ping 127.0.0.1` tests your own TCP/IP stack; `ping <default-gateway>` tests the LAN; `ping 8.8.8.8` tests internet routing without DNS; `ping google.com` adds DNS to the test. The first step that fails marks the boundary of the problem.

`tracert` (and `pathping`) shows every hop to a destination, so you can see exactly where packets die — inside your network, at the ISP, or at the far end. Rows of asterisks with eventual success usually mean a router that deprioritizes ICMP, not a broken path.

DNS failures masquerade as total outages: everything by IP works, but every name fails. `nslookup google.com` tests resolution directly, and `ipconfig /flushdns` clears a poisoned local cache. If names fail but IPs work, fix DNS — not the NIC.

example.code:
ipconfig /all
ping 127.0.0.1
ping 192.168.1.1
ping 8.8.8.8
ping google.com
tracert 8.8.8.8
nslookup google.com
ipconfig /flushdns
example.walkthrough: Read ipconfig first: confirm you have a real DHCP address and note the gateway. Then climb the ping ladder — loopback, gateway, external IP, hostname — and stop at the first failure, because that step names the broken layer. tracert shows where the path breaks beyond your LAN, nslookup isolates DNS, and flushdns clears a stale resolver cache as a last resort.

pitfalls: A failed ping does not always mean 'down' — many firewalls block ICMP while the service behind them works fine.
Seeing 169.254.x.x and 'fixing' it with a static IP in that range: APIPA never routes, so you have only hidden the DHCP failure.
Asterisks in tracert output are often routers ignoring ICMP, not dead hops — judge by whether the trace completes.
Flushing DNS fixes name resolution only; it does nothing for a DHCP or gateway problem.
lessons.try_it: Open a terminal and run the ping ladder against your own network. Write down your gateway address from ipconfig /all first, then predict which ladder step would fail if your DHCP server died — check your prediction against scenario comptia-a-plus-sc6.

lessons.title: The Windows repair toolkit: sfc, chkdsk, and Safe Mode
concepts: `sfc /scannow` (System File Checker) scans protected Windows system files and replaces corrupt ones from the component store. Run it from an elevated Command Prompt when apps crash, Windows behaves erratically, or updates fail. If sfc reports corruption it cannot fix, `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth` repairs the component store itself — then run sfc again.

`chkdsk` checks filesystem integrity: `/f` fixes logical errors, `/r` additionally locates bad sectors and recovers readable data (implying /f). Use it when Event Viewer shows disk errors or files go missing. On a suspect drive, back up data first — a dying disk can fail completely under the scan's stress — and expect `/r` to take hours on large drives.

Safe Mode boots Windows with a minimal driver set, which is the right environment for malware removal and driver troubleshooting: if the problem vanishes in Safe Mode, a third-party driver or startup item is the cause. Reach it via Settings → Recovery → Advanced startup, or `shutdown /r /o` from an elevated prompt.

Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc) is the source of truth that separates hardware from software faults. Windows Logs → System records disk, driver, and service errors with timestamps — check it before theorizing, because its entries often name the failing component outright.

System Restore rolls system files and settings back to a restore point without touching personal files — useful for bad driver or update rollouts. It is not a backup and not malware removal: the malware-removal procedure explicitly disables System Restore before remediation so infected restore points cannot re-infect the machine.

example.code:
sfc /scannow
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
chkdsk C: /r
shutdown /r /o /t 0
eventvwr
example.walkthrough: Start elevated: sfc repairs system files, and DISM repairs the store sfc draws from if sfc cannot finish the job. chkdsk /r addresses the disk surface underneath — always before trusting file repairs on a suspect drive. `shutdown /r /o` reboots into the advanced startup menu for Safe Mode or WinRE, and eventvwr opens Event Viewer so you can confirm the fault from the logs instead of guessing.

pitfalls: sfc and DISM require an elevated prompt — without it they fail or report misleading results.
chkdsk /r on a multi-terabyte drive can run for many hours; schedule it, and never run it as the first step on a drive with irreplaceable unbacked-up data.
DISM's /RestoreHealth needs internet access to fetch a healthy image unless you point it at local source media.
System Restore is disabled during malware remediation for a reason — re-enabling it too early can restore the infection.
lessons.try_it: Open Event Viewer on your own machine and read the last 24 hours of the System log. Find one warning or error, note its source and event ID, and decide whether it points at hardware or software — then check your reasoning against scenario comptia-a-plus-sc15.

labs.title: Isolate a DHCP failure with the ping ladder
labs.objective: Use ipconfig, the ping ladder, and DHCP renewal to prove a workstation's outage is a DHCP failure — not a cable, NIC, or internet problem.
steps: Open the simulated terminal and run `ipconfig`. Record the IPv4 address and note whether a default gateway is present.
Identify the address type: a 169.254.x.x address with no gateway is APIPA — Windows self-assigned because DHCP failed.
Run `ping 127.0.0.1` to verify the local TCP/IP stack is healthy independent of the network.
Run `ping 192.168.1.1` (the gateway) to test LAN reachability.
Force a fresh DHCP request with `ipconfig /release` followed by `ipconfig /renew`.
Run `ipconfig` again and document the before/after addresses plus your conclusion: DHCP failure, and whether the renew fixed it.

checks.hint: Run ipconfig and look for the APIPA address that proves DHCP failed.
Ping the loopback address (127.0.0.1) to verify the local TCP/IP stack.
Renew the DHCP lease with ipconfig /renew, then re-check the address.

labs.title: Repair system files and check disk health
labs.objective: Diagnose a crash-prone Windows machine from its event logs, then apply sfc and chkdsk in the correct order.
steps: Open the simulated terminal and launch Event Viewer with `eventvwr`.
Navigate to Windows Logs → System and look for repeated entries from the Disk source — these indicate hardware-level disk errors.
Open an elevated Command Prompt (right-click → Run as administrator) — sfc and chkdsk both require elevation.
Back up critical data first (simulated with `robocopy C:\Users\Tech\Documents D:\Backup /E`), because a suspect disk can fail under scan stress.
Run `chkdsk C: /r` to locate bad sectors and recover readable data — the disk surface must be addressed before file repairs.
Run `sfc /scannow` to repair protected Windows system files onto the now-stable disk.
Document your conclusion: whether the disk errors persist after chkdsk, and whether drive replacement is warranted.

checks.hint: Launch Event Viewer with eventvwr and open Windows Logs → System.
Run chkdsk with the /r flag on the system volume before touching system files.
Run sfc /scannow from the elevated prompt after chkdsk completes.

sections.heading: Windows admin tools & commands
items: Task Manager — Ctrl+Shift+Esc: processes, performance, startup apps
Event Viewer — eventvwr.msc: System/Application logs for diagnostics
Disk Management — diskmgmt.msc: partitions, drive letters, initialization
Device Manager — devmgmt.msc: driver status and hardware faults
System Information — msinfo32: full hardware/software inventory
System Configuration — msconfig: boot options, selective startup
sfc /scannow — repair protected Windows system files (elevated)
chkdsk C: /f — fix filesystem errors; /r — also recover bad sectors
diskpart — disk partitioning shell (list disk, clean, convert gpt)
ping / tracert / pathping — connectivity and route diagnostics
netstat -ano — listening ports and owning PIDs

sections.heading: CompTIA 6-step troubleshooting methodology
items: 1. Identify the problem — gather info, question users, check logs
2. Establish a theory of probable cause — question the obvious first
3. Test the theory to determine the cause — confirm before acting
4. Establish a plan of action and implement the solution — consider effects
5. Verify full system functionality; implement preventive measures

sections.heading: Malware removal procedure (best practice order)
items: 2. Quarantine infected systems from the network
4. Remediate — anti-malware scans, Safe Mode if needed
6. Enable System Restore and create a restore point
7. Educate the end user on prevention
